# Aortic valve stenosis

*Categories: Clinical knowledge > Internal medicine > Cardiology and angiology > Valvular heart diseases > Aortic valve stenosis*

[Original Article Link](/library/Zh0Zcf)

---

## Summary

<u>Aortic valve</u> stenosis (<u>AS</u>) is a <u>valvular heart disease</u> characterized by narrowing of the <u>aortic valve</u>. As a result, the outflow of blood from the <u>left ventricle</u> into the aorta is obstructed. This leads to chronic and progressive excess load on the <u>left ventricle</u> and potentially <u>left ventricular failure</u>. The patient may remain asymptomatic for long periods of time; for this reason, <u>AS</u> is often detected late when it first becomes symptomatic (<u>dyspnea on exertion</u>, <u>angina pectoris</u>, or <u>syncope</u>). <u>Auscultation</u> reveals a harsh, crescendo-decrescendo <u>murmur</u> in <u>systole</u> that radiates to the carotids, and pulses are delayed with diminished carotid upstrokes. <u>Echocardiography</u> is the noninvasive <u>gold standard</u> for diagnosis. Patients with mild asymptomatic aortic stenosis are <u>treated conservatively</u> with monitoring and medical management of related conditions (e.g., <u>hypertension</u>). Symptomatic patients, or those with <u>severe aortic valve stenosis</u>, require immediate <u>aortic valve replacement</u> (AVR) as definitive treatment. Options for valve replacement include surgical AVR or transcatheter AVR (<u>TAVR</u>) for patients with high operative risk. Patients with <u>severe AS</u> have a high risk of developing acute complications such as <u>heart failure</u> and <u>cardiogenic shock</u>, which are challenging to manage and often require critical care interventions and expedited <u>surgery</u> or <u>TAVR</u>.

Aortic valve stenosis fact sheet

## Epidemiology

* Most common <u>valvular heart disease</u> in industrialized countries

* Frequently associated with <u>aortic regurgitation</u>

* <u>Prevalence</u> [[1]](/library/2ZYTan)

* Increases with age

* May reach up to 12.4% among individuals ≥ 75 years




Epidemiological data refers to the US, unless otherwise specified.

---

## Etiology

The most common etiologies of valvular aortic stenosis include:




* Aortic valve sclerosis: calcification and <u>fibrosis</u> of <u>aortic valve</u> leaflets [[2]](/library/kIYm1q)

* Most common cause of aortic stenosis

* Occurs at an increasing rate as patients age (<u>prevalence</u> is 35% in those aged 75–85 years) [[3]](/library/rnbfu8)

* Similar pathophysiology to <u>atherosclerosis</u> (see <u>risk factors for atherosclerosis</u>)

* Bicuspid aortic valve (BAV): fusion of two of the three aortic-valve leaflets in utero [[2]](/library/kIYm1q)

* Most common congenital <u>heart valve</u> <u>malformation</u> , predominantly affects males (3:1) [[4]](/library/rOYfF6)

* Predisposes the valve to <u>dystrophic calcification</u> and degeneration

* Patients present with symptoms of aortic stenosis earlier than in regular <u>aortic valve</u> calcification.  [[2]](/library/kIYm1q)[[4]](/library/rOYfF6)

* Congenital aortic stenosis is rare and usually features a unicuspid or <u>bicuspid valve</u>. [[3]](/library/rnbfu8)

* <u>Rheumatic fever</u>  [[3]](/library/rnbfu8)

* Rare cause of <u>AS</u> in high-income countries due to consistent use of <u>antibiotics</u> for the treatment of <u>streptococcal pharyngitis</u>

* Still remains a significant cause of <u>AS</u> in lower-income countries, where <u>antibiotics</u> may be less readily available

* Stenosis is caused by commissural fusion. [[3]](/library/rnbfu8)





> [!TIP]
> <u>Aortic valve sclerosis</u> occurs without aortic stenosis in its early stages, but can progress to aortic stenosis once signs of <u>LVOT obstruction</u> begin to occur. [[5]](/library/JA1skj0)

---

## Pathophysiology

* Narrowed opening area of the <u>aortic valve</u> during <u>systole</u> → obstruction of blood flow from <u>left ventricle</u> (LV) → increased LV pressure → <u>left ventricular</u> <u>concentric hypertrophy</u>, which leads to:

* Increased LV oxygen demand

* Impaired <u>ventricular filling</u> during <u>diastole</u> → <u>left heart failure</u>

* Reduced coronary flow reserve

* Initially, <u>cardiac output</u> (CO) can be maintained (see “Compensation mechanisms” in “<u>Congestive heart failure</u>”)

* Later, the decreased distensibility of the <u>left ventricle</u> reduces <u>cardiac output</u> and may then cause backflow into the <u>pulmonary veins</u> and <u>capillaries</u> → higher <u>afterload</u> (pulmonic pressure) on the right <u>heart</u> → <u>right heart failure</u>





References:[[6]](/library/U30b3f)[[7]](/library/tBaXcM)

---

## Clinical features

Aortic stenosis may remain asymptomatic for years, particularly with mild or moderate stenosis. Symptoms usually start to develop when the disease progresses to <u>severe AS</u>, and may present at rest or on exertion.




* Signs and symptoms   

* <u>Dyspnea</u> (typically exertional)

* <u>Angina pectoris</u>

* <u>Dizziness</u> and <u>syncope</u>

* Additional signs specific to <u>infants</u>: <u>wheezing</u> and difficulty feeding

* <u>Physical examination</u>

* Small blood pressure amplitude, decreased <u>pulse pressure</u>

* Weak and delayed <u>distal</u> <u>pulse</u> ; (pulsus parvus et tardus) [[2]](/library/kIYm1q)

* Palpable systolic <u>thrill</u> over the bifurcation of the carotids and the aorta [[2]](/library/kIYm1q)

* See <u>cardiovascular examination</u> for further details.

* <u>Auscultation</u>

* Harsh crescendo-decrescendo (diamond-shaped), late <u>systolic ejection</u> <u>murmur</u> that radiates bilaterally to the carotids

* Best heard in the 2<sup>nd</sup> right <u>intercostal space</u>

* Handgrip decreases the intensity of the <u>murmur</u>.

* Valsalva and standing from squatting decreases or does not change the intensity of the <u>murmur</u> (in contrast to <u>hypertrophic cardiomyopathy</u>).

* See <u>auscultation in valvular defects</u> for comparison with other <u>valvular heart diseases</u>.

* Soft <u>S2</u>

* <u>S4</u> is best heard at the apex.

* Early systolic <u>ejection click</u>





> [!NOTE]
> To remember the three major symptoms of <u>aortic valve</u> stenosis, think: SAD (<u>syncope</u>, <u>angina</u>, <u>dyspnea</u>).

## Diagnosis

### Initial evaluation




#### <u>Echocardiography</u> [[9]](/library/-FXDk-)




* Indication: assessment of <u>aortic valve</u> structure, function, and stenosis severity, <u>left ventricle</u> and other <u>heart valves</u> (see “<u>Valvular heart diseases</u>”)

* <u>TTE</u>: recommended primary test;  and noninvasive <u>gold standard</u> used to confirm diagnosis and determine <u>AS</u> severity [[9]](/library/-FXDk-)

* <u>TEE</u>: second-line modality for confirmation of <u>TTE</u> findings  or operative planning  [[13]](/library/Bnbzv8)

* Supportive findings

* Calcification and narrowing of the <u>aortic valve</u>

* Increased <u>mean aortic pressure gradient</u> and transvalvular <u>velocity</u>

* Signs of <u>cardiac remodeling</u>, e.g., <u>concentric hypertrophy</u>





![Continuous wave (CW) Doppler in aortic valvular stenosis](media/q6whxum4c2g6ai2sf018mzjm.jpg)

Continuous wave (CW) Doppler in aortic valvular stenosis

![Left ventricular outflow tract diameter](media/uvsvueiuilv2zutsew6sokgj.jpg)

Left ventricular outflow tract diameter




#### Other




* <u>Laboratory studies</u>: usually nonspecific and therefore not routinely indicated; however, they can be useful for the evaluation of other possible etiologies.

* <u>BNP</u>/<u>NT-proBNP</u>  [[3]](/library/rnbfu8)[[14]](/library/ZLbZw8)

* <u>Troponin T/I</u>  [[14]](/library/ZLbZw8)[[15]](/library/-nbDD8)[[16]](/library/0Lbew8)

* <u>ECG</u> [[2]](/library/kIYm1q)[[3]](/library/rnbfu8)

* <u>ECG signs of LVH</u> (e.g., positive <u>Sokolow-Lyon index</u>)

* Nonspecific <u>ST-segment</u> and <u>T-wave</u> abnormalities

* <u>Chest x-ray</u>: Used to assess for <u>pulmonary edema</u> or other <u>causes of dyspnea</u>. [[2]](/library/kIYm1q)

* Visible calcifications within the <u>aortic valve</u> may indicate more severe disease. [[3]](/library/rnbfu8)

* Narrowing of retrocardiac space (<u>lateral</u> view)

* Signs of <u>cardiac remodeling</u> and associated <u>heart failure</u>: <u>x-ray signs of LVH</u>, <u>pulmonary congestion</u>, poststenotic dilation of the aorta





### Additional evaluation [[9]](/library/-FXDk-)




#### Low-dose <u>dobutamine stress testing</u>




* Indication: <u>stage D AS</u> with <u>LVEF</u> < 50% to determine the true anatomic severity of the stenosis

* Typical findings (in response to <u>dobutamine</u>)

* <u>Severe AS</u>: The <u>AVA</u> remains fixed, resulting in an increase in <u>transaortic velocity</u> and <u>mean aortic pressure gradient</u>.

* Moderate <u>AS</u>: The <u>AVA</u> increases as the <u>stroke volume</u> increases.





#### <u>Exercise stress testing</u>




* Indication: <u>stage C1 AS</u> and <u>stage C2 AS</u> to assess physiological changes with exercise

* Findings: exertional symptoms, e.g., <u>angina</u>, excessive <u>dyspnea</u>, <u>dizziness</u>, or <u>syncope</u>

* Interpretation: Exertional findings indicate <u>stage D AS</u>.





> [!WARNING]
> <u>Exercise stress testing</u> is contraindicated in patients with severe symptomatic <u>AS</u> (stage D).




#### <u>Cardiac catheterization</u>




* Diagnostic <u>cardiac catheterization</u>: an accurate diagnostic test for the evaluation of <u>aortic valve area</u>, <u>cardiac output</u>, and <u>mean aortic pressure gradient</u> (not routinely indicated)  [[9]](/library/-FXDk-)[[17]](/library/vX1A-20)

* Consider in symptomatic patients with inconclusive noninvasive testing or discrepancy between symptoms and noninvasive testing. [[18]](/library/Roblbu)

* Findings: similar to <u>echocardiographic</u> findings

* <u>Coronary angiography</u>

* Indications in patients undergoing:

* Valve <u>surgery</u>: preoperative cardiac risk <u>stratification</u> for patients with <u>angina</u>, reduced <u>LVEF</u>, signs of <u>ischemia</u>, or other <u>CAD</u> <u>risk factors</u>

* <u>TAVR</u>: intermediate to high risk of <u>CAD</u>

* Findings: <u>signs of CAD</u> (e.g., coronary stenosis)

* Complications: See “Complications” in <u>cardiac catheterization</u>.





#### Advanced imaging [[9]](/library/-FXDk-)[[19]](/library/6pbjqu)




Consider the following noninvasive imaging options in the perioperative assessment of patients with <u>severe AS</u>, along with expert consultation.




* <u>Cardiac CT</u>

* Used in select patients to rule out concomitant <u>CAD</u> if <u>pretest probability</u> is low

* Can quantify valve calcification

* Useful for specific measurements required prior to <u>TAVR</u>

* <u>Cardiac MRI</u>

* Provides precise information on anatomy and <u>hemodynamics</u>

* Can be helpful in evaluating severity of <u>AS</u> but is not always available

---

## Treatment

<u>AS</u> is a progressive condition that is definitively treated with <u>aortic valve replacement</u> or repair, the urgency of which depends on disease severity (see “<u>Staging aortic valve stenosis</u>”).




### Approach [[9]](/library/-FXDk-)




* Symptomatic and/or <u>severe AS</u>: <u>Aortic valve replacement</u> or repair is usually indicated.

* Asymptomatic or <u>mild-to-moderate AS</u>: usually <u>treated conservatively</u>; consider early <u>aortic valve replacement</u> in select patients.  [[20]](/library/iobJbu)

* All patients

* Provide <u>supportive care</u>: e.g., manage comorbidities (e.g., <u>hypertension</u>, <u>diabetes</u>), monitor progression with serial <u>echocardiography</u>, provide <u>IE prophylaxis</u> for at-risk patients.

* Manage <u>critical complications of AS</u> (e.g., <u>acute heart failure</u>) with individualized critical care focusing on acute stabilization and expedited surgical treatment.

* Consult cardiology and/or cardiothoracic <u>surgery</u>.





### <u>Supportive care</u>




#### Managing comorbidities [[9]](/library/-FXDk-)[[10]](/library/POaWsk)




Screen and treat all patients for <u>ASCVD risk factors</u> (see “<u>ASCVD prevention</u>”). [[9]](/library/-FXDk-)




* <u>Hypertension</u>: Follow standard <u>hypertension</u> guidelines; medication should be carefully titrated to avoid <u>hypotension</u>. See “<u>Hypertension management</u>.”

* <u>ACE inhibitors</u> may be beneficial in the prevention of <u>cardiac remodeling</u>.  [[21]](/library/job_bu)[[22]](/library/PobWXu)[[23]](/library/4ob3Xu)

* <u>Beta blockers</u> are preferable in patients with concurrent <u>coronary artery disease</u>. [[10]](/library/POaWsk)

* <u>Diuretics</u> should be avoided if the <u>left ventricle</u> is small.

* <u>Hyperlipidemia</u>

* See “<u>Lipid disorders</u>” screening and treatment recommendations.

* <u>Statins</u> are unlikely to directly prevent <u>AS</u> progression.

* <u>Diabetes mellitus</u>: See “<u>Diabetes management</u>.”  [[24]](/library/sobtWu)[[25]](/library/wpbh7u)[[26]](/library/9pbN7u)[[27]](/library/lqbvAu)





#### <u>Echocardiographic</u> monitoring [[28]](/library/_IX52z)




* Regular follow-up imaging is indicated for asymptomatic patients with:

* Mild <u>stage B AS</u>: every 3–5 years

* Moderate <u>stage B AS</u>: every 1–2 years

* Any stage C <u>AS</u>: every 6–12 months

* On-demand imaging is indicated for patients with:

* Any change in signs or symptoms

* Conditions that have high hemodynamic/metabolic demands





#### Prophylactic <u>antibiotics</u> [[28]](/library/_IX52z)




* <u>Rheumatic heart disease</u>: Patients should receive secondary prophylaxis, e.g., <u>penicillin G</u> benzathine DOSAGE or <u>sulfadiazine</u> DOSAGE (see “Prevention” in “<u>Rheumatic fever</u>” for more details). [[29]](/library/kobmXu)

* Dental procedures: Consider <u>prophylaxis for infective endocarditis</u> for at-risk patients (e.g., after <u>aortic valve replacement</u>).

* Nondental procedures (e.g., <u>EGD</u>, <u>TEE</u>, <u>colonoscopy</u>): <u>Antibiotic prophylaxis</u> is not recommended.





### Aortic valve replacement (AVR) and repair [[9]](/library/-FXDk-)




#### Indications




* Symptomatic patients with severe, high-gradient <u>AS</u> (<u>stage D AS</u>)

* Asymptomatic patients with <u>severe AS</u> and:

* Significantly ↓ <u>LVEF</u> (<u>stage C2 AS</u>)

* Undergoing cardiac <u>surgery</u> for other indications (stage C <u>AS</u> or <u>stage D AS</u>)

* AVR can also be beneficial for certain patients with moderate (<u>stage B AS</u>) to severe (<u>stage D AS</u>)  with specific characteristics.





> [!TIP]
> The presence of exertional symptoms (<u>dyspnea on exertion</u>, <u>angina pectoris</u>, <u>syncope</u>) is an indication for <u>surgery</u>.




#### Procedure




The choice of valve type and procedure approach involves <u>shared decision-making</u> based on multiple factors (e.g., anticoagulation risks, age, <u>life expectancy</u>). Refer candidates to a specialized <u>heart valve</u> team.  [[9]](/library/-FXDk-)




* Surgical AVR (SAVR) is recommended for patients with:

* Age < 65 years

* <u>Life expectancy</u> > 20 years

* Low to moderate surgical risk

* Transcatheter AVR (<u>TAVR</u>)

* Recommended for patients with:

* Age > 80 years

* <u>Life expectancy</u> < 10 years

* High or prohibitive surgical risk and predicted survival of > 12 months [[9]](/library/-FXDk-)

* Emergency <u>TAVR</u> may be considered in certain patient groups.  [[30]](/library/Jnbs88)[[31]](/library/qnbC88)[[32]](/library/tnbXE8)

* <u>Percutaneous balloon valvuloplasty</u> [[9]](/library/-FXDk-)

* May be used in children, <u>adolescents</u>, and young adults

* Limited role in older patients

* Can consider as a bridging intervention in high-risk patients with <u>stage D AS</u>  but overall benefit is questionable.  [[9]](/library/-FXDk-)





#### Complications of <u>aortic valve replacement</u> [[33]](/library/VIbGbE)[[34]](/library/2IbTXE)[[35]](/library/fIbkXE)




* Vascular complications, <u>thromboembolism</u>/<u>stroke</u>

* <u>Major bleeding</u>

* <u>Renal failure</u>

* <u>Arrhythmias</u>: <u>atrioventricular block</u>, <u>atrial fibrillation</u>

* <u>Aortic regurgitation</u>/paravalvular leak

* Infection: <u>endocarditis</u>





#### <u>Antithrombotic therapy</u> after <u>aortic valve replacement</u>




| <br>Antithrombotic therapy for patients with prosthetic aortic valves [[9]](/library/-FXDk-)<br> |  |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
|  | Choice of agent | Target <u>INR</u> | Duration of therapy |
| <br><u>Mechanical valve</u> and no <u>risk factors</u> for <u>thromboembolism</u> <br> | <br><br>* <u>VKA</u> is recommended, e.g., <u>warfarin</u> DOSAGE<br><br>* Addition of <u>antiplatelet agent</u>, e.g., <u>ASA</u> DOSAGE, may be considered if bleeding risk is low.<br><br><br> | <br>* 2.5 (range 2.0–3.0)<br><br> | <br>* Lifelong<br><br> |
| <br><u>Mechanical valve</u> and ≥ 1 <u>risk factor</u> for <u>thromboembolism</u>   OR older generation <u>mechanical valves</u><br> | <br>* 3.0 (range 2.5–3.5)<br><br> |  |  |
| <u>Bioprosthetic valve</u> with low risk of bleeding | <br><br>* <u>Antiplatelet agent</u> is reasonable, e.g., <u>ASA</u> DOSAGE<br><br>* Addition of a <u>VKA</u> is reasonable, e.g., <u>warfarin</u> DOSAGE<br><br><br> | <br>* 2.5 (range 2.0–3.0)<br><br> | <br><br>* <u>Antiplatelet agents</u>: lifelong<br><br>* <u>VKAs</u>: 3–6 months after SAVR or <u>TAVR</u><br><br><br> |





> [!WARNING]
> The safety and <u>efficacy</u> of <u>DOACs</u> in patients with <u>mechanical valves</u> have not been assessed and their use is not recommended. [[9]](/library/-FXDk-)




> [!WARNING]
> <u>Dabigatran</u> results in more <u>thrombotic events</u> and bleeding complications in patients with valvulopathy than <u>warfarin</u>. [[9]](/library/-FXDk-)

---

## Prognosis

* Asymptomatic patients: <u>Mortality rate</u> is < 1% in a given year. [[24]](/library/sobtWu)

* Symptomatic patients

* <u>Mortality rate</u> in the first 2 years is > 50% if left untreated. [[39]](/library/gIbFXE)

* The worst prognosis is seen in patients with <u>symptoms of heart failure</u>, followed by <u>syncope</u>, and <u>angina pectoris</u>. [[40]](/library/dSdoA60)
